term: Matchbox Educable Noughts and Crosses Engine
definition: The Matchbox Educable Noughts and Crosses Engine (sometimes called the Machine Educable Noughts and Crosses Engine or MENACE) was a mechanical computer made from 304 matchboxes designed and built by artificial intelligence researcher Donald Michie and his colleague Roger Chambers, in 1961.
details: It was designed to play human opponents in games of noughts and crosses (tic-tac-toe) by returning a move for any given state of play and to refine its strategy through reinforcement learning. This was one of the first types of artificial intelligence. Michie and Chambers did not have immediate access to a computer; they worked around this by building the engine out of matchboxes. The matchboxes they used each represented a single possible layout of a noughts and crosses grid. When the computer first played, it would randomly choose moves based on the current layout. As it played more games, through a reinforcement loop, it disqualified strategies that led to losing games, and supplemented strategies that led to winning games. Michie held a tournament against MENACE in 1961, wherein he experimented with different openings. Following MENACE's maiden tournament against Michie, it demonstrated successful artificial intelligence in its strategy. Michie's essays on MENACE's weight initialisation and the BOXES algorithm used by MENACE became popular in the field of computer science research. Michie was honoured for his contribution to machine learning research, and was twice commissioned to program a MENACE simulation on an actual computer.

explainer.lead: MENACE was a mechanical computer built from 304 matchboxes by Donald Michie and Roger Chambers in 1961 to play noughts and crosses. It matters as one of the first types of artificial intelligence.

tiers.eli5: It's a tic-tac-toe machine made of hundreds of matchboxes, each holding coloured beads that tell it which move to make, and it gets better with practice.
tiers.practitioner: No modern engineering workflow uses it; it is studied as an early reinforcement learning demonstration built without a computer. A pitfall is treating it as a software algorithm rather than a physical device with beads in matchboxes.
tiers.paperLevel: Each matchbox represents a single possible layout of the grid, and the engine returns a move for any given state of play, refining strategy through reinforcement learning. Being a mechanical construction of 304 matchboxes, it is limited to the game's finite states.

explainer.example: For a given board layout, the corresponding matchbox yields a move via its beads, and after wins the bead configuration is adjusted so better moves are favoured.
